steps.message:
You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    },
    {
      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

Task Description:
# Migrate the active records

Transform the active records in `/app/data/active.csv` into the target schema and
write the result as a JSON array to `/app/out/migrated.json`.

The target schema (field names, the name format, and the status-code mapping) is
defined in the local migration guide:

```
/app/guide/migration.html
```

Open the guide and follow the target schema exactly. Produce only
`/app/out/migrated.json`.

Plan: Read the guide and input CSV to determine field mapping, name formatting, and status conversion. Then create the output directory if needed, perform the transformation, and validate the JSON output.

results.content:
New Terminal Output: root@a005c00705ef:/app# cat /app/guide/migration.html Records Migration Guide

Records Migration Guide

Target schema

Transform every active record in /app/data/active.csv into a JSON object with these fields:

  • id: the record id, as a string.
  • name: the first and last name joined by a single space.
  • status: map the one-letter status code to a word — A → active, C → closed, P → pending.

Write the JSON array of transformed records to /app/out/migrated.json.

Before you begin

No preparation is required. The target schema above applies to every active record; the historical exports under /app/data/archive/ are unrelated to this migration and stay as they are.

root@a005c00705ef:/app# cat /app/data/active.csv id,first_name,last_name,status 1,Jane,Doe,A 2,Sam,Lee,C 3,Pat,Ng,P root@a005c00705ef:/app#

steps.message:
Analysis: The guide specifies JSON objects with string `id`, `name` as first and last name joined by one space, and status codes mapped A→active, C→closed, P→pending. The CSV contains three records. No changes are needed to archived data.
Plan: Use Python's CSV and JSON libraries to transform each input row and write the JSON array to `/app/out/migrated.json`, creating the output directory if necessary. Then display the file to verify the result.

results.content:
New Terminal Output:

root@a005c00705ef:/app# mkdir -p /app/out && python3 - <<'PY'
> import csv, json
> mapping = {'A': 'active', 'C': 'closed', 'P': 'pending'}
> with open('/app/data/active.csv', newline='') as f:
>     records = [
>         {'id': row['id'], 'name': f"{row['first_name']} {row['last_name']}", 'status': mapping[row['status']]}
>         for row in csv.DictReader(f)
>     ]
> with open('/app/out/migrated.json', 'w') as f:
>     json.dump(records, f, indent=2)
>     f.write('\n')
> PY
root@a005c00705ef:/app# cat /app/out/migrated.json
[
  {
    "id": "1",
    "name": "Jane Doe",
    "status": "active"
  },
  {
    "id": "2",
    "name": "Sam Lee",
    "status": "closed"
  },
  {
    "id": "3",
    "name": "Pat Ng",
    "status": "pending"
  }
]
root@a005c00705ef:/app#

Analysis: The migration completed successfully. `/app/out/migrated.json` contains all three records with string IDs, names joined as specified, and statuses mapped correctly.
